subtopic_detail: Recognising myocarditis in the first weeks of clozapine titration
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32 year old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia now on day 18 of clozapine titration, currently at 250 mg nocte. He was admitted this morning after his community mental health nurse noticed him looking pale and unwell. He describes three days of malaise, low grade fever, and mild shortness of breath on exertion. His neutrophil count from yesterday was within the accepted range.

He denies chest pain but says his heart is racing all the time.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 122, blood pressure 110/70, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 38.1
data_table.Cardiovascular: no murmurs, JVP not raised, no peripheral oedema, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.ECG: sinus tachycardia rate 122, no ST changes, no PR prolongation
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): troponin I 128 ng/L (<15), CRP 88 mg/L (<5), white cells 8.4 x10^9/L, neutrophils 4.6 x10^9/L, eosinophils 0.6 x10^9/L (0-0.5)
data_table.Chest X-ray: no consolidation, cardiothoracic ratio at upper limit of normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Cease clozapine and commence intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily empirically for immune myocarditis without waiting for echocardiogram results
options.rationale: Empirical high-dose steroids for clozapine myocarditis without confirmed left ventricular dysfunction is not standard care - management is drug cessation, supportive care, cardiology review and consideration of heart failure therapy if reduced ejection fraction. Steroid use is contested. (Source: RANZCP clozapine)

options.text: Continue clozapine at current dose, attribute the fever to intercurrent viral illness, and prescribe paracetamol 1 g four-hourly with review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Missing early clozapine-induced myocarditis is fatal (mortality up to 30 percent if unrecognised). Attributing fever to viral illness in the myocarditis window without troponin testing is negligent; the raised troponin and eosinophilia here rule this out. (Source: RANZCP clozapine)

options.text: Reduce clozapine dose by 50 percent, arrange full blood count and daily observations, and defer any structural cardiac assessment unless clinical deterioration occurs
options.rationale: Dose reduction is not appropriate management of clozapine myocarditis - the drug must be ceased. Structural cardiac assessment (echocardiogram) is required immediately, not deferred. (Source: RANZCP clozapine)

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately, arrange urgent echocardiogram and cardiology review for suspected clozapine-induced myocarditis, and admit for cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Clozapine-induced myocarditis typically presents in weeks 2-4 of titration with fever, tachycardia, dyspnoea, malaise, elevated CRP, elevated troponin and often eosinophilia. Any suspicion mandates immediate cessation, urgent echocardiogram, cardiology involvement, and cardiac monitoring. Even with normal ECG the raised troponin and eosinophilia are consistent with the AU Clozapine Monitoring Protocol (Northwick Park style adopted by state HHS clozapine services) and cessation is time-critical - continued exposure kills. (Source: RANZCP clozapine)

options.text: Interpret this as clozapine-induced fever benign syndrome (constitutional response to titration) and continue drug with symptomatic management
options.rationale: Isolated benign clozapine fever without cardiac or infective source is a diagnosis of exclusion made after cardiac and infective workup. Raised troponin excludes benign fever - the diagnosis here is myocarditis. (Source: RANZCP clozapine)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis occurs in around 3 percent of Australian initiations and clusters between days 14 and 28 of titration. Presentation is non-specific: fever, tachycardia disproportionate to fever, malaise, dyspnoea, chest discomfort, sometimes eosinophilia. Australian clozapine protocols mandate baseline troponin and CRP, then weekly for 4 weeks, then as clinically indicated. Any of the following triggers immediate cessation and cardiac evaluation: troponin more than double the upper limit, CRP >100 mg/L, tachycardia >120 sustained, unexplained fever, chest pain, or heart failure signs. Management is drug cessation, echocardiogram, cardiology involvement, and heart failure therapy if LV dysfunction develops. Re-challenge is only in specialist settings after full recovery and multidisciplinary discussion.
key_points: Days 14-28 of titration is the peak window
Fever, tachycardia disproportionate to fever, malaise, eosinophilia, troponin/CRP rise
Cease clozapine, urgent echocardiogram, cardiology, cardiac monitoring
Weekly troponin/CRP for the first 4 weeks per AU protocols
Re-challenge only in specialist setting after MDT discussion
explanation.pearls: Clozapine cardiomyopathy is a separate later complication (months to years after initiation) presenting with progressive heart failure symptoms; annual echocardiography is recommended for long-term clozapine-treated patients under AU protocols.

subtopic_detail: Bush-Francis features, lorazepam challenge, and ECT escalation
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 40 year old woman admitted three days ago with dehydration and poor oral intake. She is well known to psychiatric services with bipolar I disorder and has had two previous manic episodes on lithium prophylaxis. The medical team say she is lying immobile and unable to answer questions today. On examination she holds an odd position when the examiner moves her arm and echoes fragments of what you say.

She passively resists any attempt to move her limbs and does not respond to commands.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Bush-Francis features observed: mutism, stupor, waxy flexibility, echolalia, negativism, staring, immobility
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): sodium 141 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 8.9 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, creatine kinase 480 U/L (<200), TSH 2.4 mIU/L, ammonia normal
data_table.Recent medications: lithium 750 mg nocte (level 0.72 mmol/L), no antipsychotics, no recent dopamine antagonists

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Administer IV lorazepam 2 mg and reassess Bush-Francis score at 15 minutes, with escalation to a repeat dose if partial response and ECT if refractory
options.rationale: Catatonia is clinically diagnosed with three or more of 12 Bush-Francis features (mutism, stupor, waxy flexibility, echolalia, negativism, staring, posturing, grimacing, immobility, mannerisms, echopraxia, stereotypy - this patient has seven). The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV) is both diagnostic and therapeutic: 60-80 percent respond within 30 minutes with reduction in Bush-Francis score, confirming catatonia. First-line ongoing management is scheduled lorazepam (usually 8-24 mg/day). ECT is indicated if lorazepam fails or in malignant catatonia. (Source: RANZCP catatonia)

options.text: Commence intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg for underlying manic state given prior bipolar I diagnosis and immediately observed odd behaviour
options.rationale: Antipsychotics in undiagnosed catatonia risk precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome and worsening the catatonic state. Lorazepam is first-line before any dopamine antagonist is considered. (Source: RANZCP catatonia)

options.text: Immediate empirical intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g for possible autoimmune encephalitis and defer psychiatric intervention until autoantibody panel returns
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis is a differential but is not the initial move without more directive clinical or CSF findings. Lorazepam challenge is safe and diagnostic in typical catatonia; autoantibody workup runs in parallel if there are red flags (focal neurology, seizures, autonomic instability). (Source: RANZCP catatonia)

options.text: Perform urgent lumbar puncture and start empirical intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg eight-hourly for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis
options.rationale: There are no signs of encephalitis (no fever spike, no seizures, no focal neurology, no CSF concerns). Lorazepam challenge is the appropriate first-line diagnostic. LP may follow if features evolve. (Source: RANZCP catatonia)

options.text: Increase lithium to 1000 mg nocte to treat presumed underlying bipolar episode and observe for improvement over 72 hours before re-evaluating
options.rationale: Lithium acts too slowly (weeks) to treat catatonia, and dose escalation in a patient with reduced oral intake risks toxicity. Lorazepam is the specific first-line intervention. (Source: RANZCP catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome, not a diagnosis - it complicates severe affective disorders (most commonly bipolar depression and mania), psychotic disorders, medical illness (autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic derangement), and drug effects (steroids, dopamine antagonists). Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale scores three or more of 12 signs. The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV or IM) is diagnostic and therapeutic - 60-80 percent respond within 30 minutes. Failure to respond does not exclude catatonia; escalate to ECT which is highly effective. Antipsychotics risk precipitating malignant catatonia/NMS and are avoided until catatonia is treated. Underlying cause (medical, psychiatric) is investigated and treated in parallel.
key_points: Bush-Francis: 3+ of 12 features (mutism, stupor, waxy flexibility, etc.)
Lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV) diagnostic + therapeutic
60-80% respond in 30 min; escalate scheduled lorazepam then ECT if refractory
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia is treated (NMS risk)
Investigate underlying medical, autoimmune, and psychiatric cause
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (catatonia plus autonomic instability, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis) has mortality up to 30 percent and is a psychiatric emergency requiring ECT within 24 hours; benzodiazepines are a bridge but ECT is the definitive intervention.

subtopic: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome
subtopic_detail: Discriminating features and immediate management divergence
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 46 year old man brought in by his housemate with three hours of agitation and shaking. He has depression on sertraline 200 mg daily and started tramadol 50 mg four-hourly three days ago after a work back injury. His housemate reports he has been taking St John's wort for chronic pain and just started olanzapine yesterday for anxiety, prescribed by another GP.

On examination he is tremulous, sweating profusely and unable to keep still.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 168/108, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Neurological: sustained lower limb clonus, hyperreflexia (patellar 4+, ankle 4+), inducible clonus in upper limbs, tremor
data_table.Mental state: agitated, restless, confused, mydriasis 5 mm bilaterally
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): creatine kinase 640 U/L (<200), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, urea 6.4 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, white cells 11 x10^9/L
data_table.Onset: over hours after new drug additions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give IV bromocriptine 2.5 mg via nasogastric tube every 8 hours to reverse presumed dopamine blockade underlying the neuroleptic malignant syndrome features
options.rationale: Bromocriptine treats NMS by reversing dopamine blockade; it is not indicated in serotonin syndrome and could worsen it. The temporal pattern (hours, not days after antipsychotic) and clonus (not rigidity) point to serotonin toxicity. (Source: eTG Complete Toxicology)

options.text: Continue sertraline and olanzapine, add IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg for muscle rigidity, and admit for cardiac monitoring under general medicine
options.rationale: Continuing the serotonergic drugs is the opposite of what is needed. Dantrolene is used in malignant hyperthermia and adjunctive in severe NMS, not first-line in serotonin syndrome. Rigidity here is clonic, not the lead-pipe rigidity of NMS. (Source: eTG Complete Toxicology)

options.text: Cease all serotonergic drugs, administer IV midazolam 5 mg titrated for agitation, cool actively, and start IV crystalloid; consider cyproheptadine 12 mg orally if severe features persist
options.rationale: The features (rapid onset over hours after adding tramadol and olanzapine to sertraline plus St John's wort, tremor, hyperreflexia with sustained lower limb clonus greater than upper limb, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds if elicited, autonomic instability) fit the Hunter serotonin toxicity criteria. Management is cessation of serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, tramadol, St John's wort), aggressive benzodiazepine sedation for autonomic instability and muscle activity, active cooling, IV fluids, and cyproheptadine (5HT2A antagonist) for refractory cases. NMS presents more slowly (days to weeks after antipsychotic exposure) with rigidity (not clonus), hyporeflexia, normal pupils. (Source: eTG Complete Toxicology)

options.text: Give IV benztropine 2 mg for suspected acute dystonic reaction from newly commenced olanzapine and observe over the next hour for resolution
options.rationale: Acute dystonia presents with focal muscle spasm (oculogyric crisis, torticollis, trismus), not autonomic instability, clonus and fever. Benztropine has no role in serotonin syndrome. (Source: eTG Complete Toxicology)

options.text: Empirically commence intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and aciclovir 10 mg/kg for suspected meningoencephalitis before further diagnostics in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: The clinical picture (drug additions, hyperreflexia and clonus, mydriasis, no headache/neck stiffness/rash) is drug toxicity, not CNS infection. Empirical antibiotics delay specific management. (Source: eTG Complete Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is a clinical diagnosis based on Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria: in a patient exposed to a serotonergic agent, one of - spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, tremor with hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature >38 and clonus. Onset is within hours of drug addition; features include neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor), autonomic instability (fever, tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, diaphoresis, hyperactive bowel sounds), and altered mental state. NMS by contrast develops over days to weeks after dopamine antagonist exposure with lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, fever, autonomic instability. Management of serotonin syndrome: cease serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepine sedation, aggressive cooling and IV fluids, cyproheptadine for severe cases.
key_points: Hunter criteria: clonus + hyperreflexia + agitation/diaphoresis in serotonergic patient
Onset over hours (SS) vs days-weeks (NMS)
Clonus + hyperreflexia (SS) vs lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia (NMS)
Cease serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepines, cooling, IV fluids; cyproheptadine for severe
Mydriasis in SS; pupils typically normal in NMS
explanation.pearls: Tramadol and pethidine both have serotonergic activity and are frequently overlooked culprits when added to SSRIs; fentanyl is a safer opioid choice in patients on SSRIs when acute analgesia is needed.

subtopic_detail: Electrolyte monitoring and phosphate replacement in refeeding
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 19 year old woman transferred from a specialist eating disorders unit for medical refeeding. She has anorexia nervosa restricting subtype for 3 years with recent rapid deterioration. Her weight today is 34 kg (BMI 12.4) with 16 percent weight loss over the last 6 weeks. She has been taking around 400 kcal a day for the past 4 weeks. She is medically compliant but ambivalent about weight restoration.

Her parents have accompanied her and she has provided informed consent to the medical management plan.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 42, blood pressure 82/54 (drop of 20 mmHg systolic on standing), respiratory rate 12, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 35.6
data_table.ECG: sinus bradycardia rate 42, QTc 490 ms, no ST changes
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.65 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.80-1.50), glucose 3.4 mmol/L, urea 5.2 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, albumin 32 g/L
data_table.Nutritional intake last week: ~400 kcal per day of restricted intake

lead_in: What is the most appropriate refeeding plan for the first 72 hours?

options.text: Begin refeeding at 30 kcal/kg/day with rapid escalation to full requirement within 48 hours to achieve early weight gain given severity of malnutrition
options.rationale: Rapid refeeding in severe malnutrition (BMI under 13, recent rapid weight loss, minimal recent intake) causes refeeding syndrome (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, cardiac failure, arrhythmia, neurological complications, death). Australian guidance is to start at 10-20 kcal/kg/day with gradual escalation, close electrolyte monitoring, and prophylactic phosphate and thiamine. (Source: ANZAED refeeding guidelines)

options.text: Commence total parenteral nutrition at 25 kcal/kg/day to bypass the gastrointestinal tract entirely and secure nutritional delivery
options.rationale: TPN is reserved for patients who cannot use the GI tract (obstruction, malabsorption). Enteral feeding is preferred where the gut works. TPN is associated with catheter sepsis and biochemical instability and is not first-line for anorexia nervosa refeeding. (Source: ANZAED refeeding guidelines)

options.text: Withhold all feeding for 48 hours until electrolytes fully normalise, then start slow feeding once biochemistry is corrected to reduce the refeeding risk
options.rationale: Delaying feeding entirely in a critically malnourished patient worsens outcomes because ongoing starvation depletes reserves further. The correct approach is careful low-rate refeeding with intensive electrolyte support, not fasting. (Source: ANZAED refeeding guidelines)

options.text: Insert nasogastric tube and commence continuous feeding at 40 mL/hour of standard 1 kcal/mL feed with once-weekly electrolyte checks throughout the admission
options.rationale: 40 mL/hour of 1 kcal/mL = 960 kcal/day, exceeding the 10-20 kcal/kg/day (340-680 kcal/day at 34 kg) initial target. Weekly bloods are inadequate - daily electrolytes are needed for at least 5 days in high-risk patients. (Source: ANZAED refeeding guidelines)

options.text: Start refeeding at 10 to 20 kcal/kg/day with immediate IV thiamine 300 mg daily, prophylactic phosphate and multivitamin supplementation, daily bloods (K, PO4, Mg, glucose)
options.rationale: Australian guidance (ANZAED, ABC-2020 update from MARSIPAN) for severe malnutrition (BMI <13 or rapid loss >15 percent, low intake, biochemistry already at low reference range) recommends starting at 10-20 kcal/kg/day, giving IV thiamine 300 mg daily before feeds start (Wernicke prophylaxis), prophylactic phosphate (Phosphate Sandoz orally or IV Addiphos), K/Mg replacement to keep levels mid-range, daily electrolytes for 5 days then alternate days, continuous cardiac monitoring for at least 5 days, and specialist eating disorder consultation. (Source: ANZAED refeeding guidelines)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the acute biochemical decompensation (severe hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, thiamine deficiency, glucose intolerance, cardiac failure) that occurs when carbohydrate is reintroduced to a starved patient. Insulin surge drives intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium; thiamine is consumed in glucose metabolism. Deaths occur within days of refeeding when this is not anticipated. Australian ANZAED/ABC-2020 guidance for severe malnutrition: start 10-20 kcal/kg/day, give IV thiamine 300 mg daily before feed, prophylactic phosphate and multivitamin, daily K/PO4/Mg/Ca/glucose for 5 days, continuous cardiac monitoring for 5 days, specialist eating disorder team, gradual increase over 5-7 days to full requirement, weight gain target 0.5-1 kg/week. Involuntary admission under the state mental health act may be required if capacity is lost.
key_points: Start 10-20 kcal/kg/day, escalate over 5-7 days
IV thiamine 300 mg daily BEFORE feeds (Wernicke prevention)
Prophylactic phosphate + multivitamin; K/Mg replaced to mid-range
Daily electrolytes for 5 days, continuous cardiac monitoring 5 days
Specialist eating disorder team; consider Mental Health Act if capacity lost
explanation.pearls: A prolonged QTc in severe anorexia nervosa is more often multifactorial (hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, low T3) than structural; replacement of electrolytes and thyroid stabilisation with refeeding typically normalises the QTc without cardiology intervention.

subtopic: Borderline personality disorder in emergency care
subtopic_detail: Structured discharge planning after intentional self-injury
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 28 year old woman with a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder who presented with multiple superficial lacerations to her forearms after an argument with her partner. Her wounds have been cleaned and steristripped by the nurses. She is well known to community mental health with regular dialectical behaviour therapy sessions. She denies current suicidal intent and says she wants to go home.

Her usual mental health case manager has just responded that she can offer a review tomorrow morning.

data_table.Mental state: distressed but engaging, no psychosis, no acute suicidal ideation or plan, chronic passive suicidal ideation only
data_table.Wounds: multiple superficial parallel lacerations bilateral forearms, all closed, no need for further intervention
data_table.Substance use: no acute intoxication, urinary drug screen negative
data_table.Risk factors: high previous self-harm frequency, one past overdose 2 years ago, in DBT program with good engagement
data_table.Social: partner supportive, lives with partner, community mental health case manager available tomorrow

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home with a written safety plan co-produced with her, confirmed community mental health follow-up within 24 hours, and information about crisis lines
options.rationale: Structured discharge with a personalised written safety plan (identifying triggers, coping strategies, distraction techniques, contacts and 24-hour crisis lines), confirmed rapid community mental health follow-up (within 24-48 hours), and reinforcement of her existing DBT skills is the evidence-based response for chronic self-injury in BPD without acute suicidal intent. Admission increases dependency, disrupts DBT progress and does not reduce longer-term risk. (Source: RANZCP borderline personality disorder)

options.text: Admit under psychiatry involuntarily under the state Mental Health Act for at least 72 hours of intensive risk assessment and containment
options.rationale: Involuntary admission requires evidence of severely disordered decision-making capacity or imminent risk not manageable in the community. Chronic self-injury without acute intent does not meet criteria. Repeated admissions worsen BPD outcomes and undermine therapeutic work. (Source: RANZCP borderline personality disorder)

options.text: Prescribe olanzapine 10 mg IM in the ED to sedate her acute distress and reduce the immediate risk of further self-harm before disposition
options.rationale: Pharmacological sedation of a non-agitated distressed patient with BPD is not therapeutic and can medicalise emotional dysregulation. Guidelines advise against routine pharmacotherapy for the core features of BPD; only comorbid conditions and short-term distress are targets. (Source: RANZCP borderline personality disorder)

options.text: Refer to inpatient dialectical behaviour therapy as day-only intensive intervention for one week to intensify treatment for recurrent self-injury
options.rationale: DBT is delivered in structured weekly group and individual outpatient sessions over months to years; an inpatient DBT intensive is not the standard AU care model for chronic self-injury without acute crisis. Rapid outpatient follow-up with her existing DBT team is optimal. (Source: RANZCP borderline personality disorder)

options.text: Discharge home with a prescription for lorazepam 1 mg orally three times daily as required for the next week to manage distress-related self-injury urges
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines in BPD carry disinhibition, dependency and overdose risks. RANZCP guidance advises against routine PRN benzodiazepine prescribing for distress in BPD; skills-based crisis planning is safer and more effective. (Source: RANZCP borderline personality disorder)

explanation.summary: Emergency management of self-injury in BPD focuses on medical care of the wound, brief structured risk assessment, collaborative safety planning, warm handover to community mental health services, and reinforcement of existing therapeutic work. Admission is reserved for acute suicidal intent not manageable in the community, severe comorbidity, or protective needs during a specific crisis. Routine admission of chronic self-injury worsens outcomes by reinforcing dependency, disrupting DBT skills work, and exposing the patient to iatrogenic harms. Safety planning is a specific intervention (Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention) - written, personalised, collaborative, identifying warning signs, coping strategies, contacts, and means restriction.
key_points: Structured safety plan + rapid community follow-up outperforms admission for chronic BPD self-injury
Admission reserved for acute intent not manageable in the community
Avoid routine benzodiazepines and PRN sedation in BPD
Reinforce existing DBT skills; do not disrupt outpatient work
Involuntary treatment threshold applies same as other conditions
explanation.pearls: The Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention (SPI) is a six-step written plan (warning signs, internal coping, social contacts and settings, people to help, professional agencies, means restriction) shown in AU cohorts to reduce re-presentation over the following 6 months when combined with rapid follow-up.

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic and dexamethasone timing before lumbar puncture
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department assessing a 24 year old university student brought in by her housemates after two days of headache, fever and increasing confusion this morning. She has never been unwell before and takes no regular medications. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable. There is meningism on examination and a purpuric rash is developing on her lower legs.

She has had one seizure witnessed by paramedics 20 minutes ago that self-terminated within a minute.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% on 6 L Hudson, temperature 39.4
data_table.Neurological: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), no focal deficit, neck stiffness present, photophobia
data_table.Skin: spreading non-blanching purpura on lower legs and forearms
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): white cells 18 x10^9/L, platelets 128 x10^9/L, CRP 220 mg/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, INR 1.4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Perform urgent lumbar puncture before any antibiotic administration to preserve CSF culture yield and guide targeted therapy in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in the presence of reduced GCS, focal neurological deficit, seizure, coagulopathy or haemodynamic instability without prior imaging, and antibiotics must not be delayed by LP or imaging. Every hour of delay in bacterial meningitis increases mortality. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - meningitis)

options.text: Give IV mannitol 1 g/kg over 30 minutes for raised intracranial pressure and intubate to protect airway before considering antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Airway protection may be needed if GCS falls further, but empirical antibiotics and dexamethasone must not be delayed. Mannitol is used for confirmed raised ICP with imaging or clinical evidence of impending herniation, not empirically. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - meningitis)

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin 1 g eight-hourly and admit to the medical ward for observation while awaiting CT and LP results tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics for bacterial meningitis are inadequate. Admission to the medical ward without ICU-level care in a shocked, seizing patient with meningism and purpura is negligent. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - meningitis)

options.text: Empirically start intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours alone for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis and defer bacterial cover until CSF results are available
options.rationale: Purpuric rash and rapid onset with meningism points to bacterial meningitis (meningococcal, pneumococcal). Aciclovir may be added if HSV encephalitis is a differential but does not replace bacterial cover. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - meningitis)

options.text: Administer IV dexamethasone 10 mg immediately followed by IV ceftriaxone 2 g and benzylpenicillin 2.4 g (or replace with vancomycin if pneumococcal resistance concerns), then proceed
options.rationale: In suspected bacterial meningitis in adults the eTG-recommended empirical regimen is IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly (to cover Listeria in >50 years or immunocompromised) with IV dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly for 4 days ideally given before or with the first antibiotic dose (reduces pneumococcal mortality and neurological sequelae). Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin is used if pneumococcal resistance is a concern. LP is deferred until GCS improves and coagulopathy is corrected. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - meningitis)

explanation.summary: Suspected bacterial meningitis in an adult requires antibiotic administration within one hour of presentation - imaging and lumbar puncture must not delay this. Empirical AU regimen is IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly (adds Listeria cover for over 50 or immunocompromised; vancomycin substitutes if pneumococcal resistance is likely). IV dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly for 4 days is given with or before the first antibiotic to reduce mortality and neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. LP is deferred if reduced GCS, focal neurology, seizure, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, or haemodynamic instability - CT first, then LP once safe. Public health notification for meningococcal disease is immediate; household contacts require rifampicin or ciprofloxacin prophylaxis.
key_points: Antibiotics within 1 hour of presentation; do not delay for imaging or LP
IV ceftriaxone 2 g + benzylpenicillin 2.4 g (add vancomycin if resistance concern)
IV dexamethasone 10 mg with or before the first antibiotic dose
LP deferred if reduced GCS, focal deficit, seizure, coagulopathy
Public health notification + contact prophylaxis for meningococcal
explanation.pearls: In an unwell patient in whom pneumococcal resistance is a concern (recent travel, prior beta-lactam use, immunocompromised), add IV vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg loading; the AMR rate for penicillin-resistant pneumococcus in Australia remains low but rising in specific populations.
